summary: On Tuesday, Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in New York Attorney General Letitia James' civil lawsuit that Donald Trump and the Trump Organization committed fraud by massively overvaluing assets and exaggerating net worth on financial statements to obtain favorable loans and insurance terms. He ordered some business licenses rescinded and continued independent monitoring of the company. Six other claims remain for a non-jury trial starting Oct. 2, where James seeks $250 million in penalties and a ban on Trump doing business in New York.
one_line: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled Donald Trump and his company committed fraud by inflating asset values, resolving the key claim in Letitia James' New York lawsuit.
key_facts: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled on Tuesday (Sept. 26, 2023) in a summary judgment that Donald Trump and the Trump Organization committed fraud by overvaluing assets and exaggerating net worth on financial statements.
Engoron ordered some of Trump's business licenses rescinded and said an independent monitor would continue to oversee the Trump Organization's operations.
In his 35-page ruling, Engoron wrote that the defendants' view of valuation 'is a fantasy world, not the real world.'
The judge rejected Trump's argument that a disclaimer on the financial statements absolved him, saying it made clear Trump was fully responsible for the information in them.
The ruling resolves the key claim in Letitia James' lawsuit, but six other claims remain; a non-jury trial starts Oct. 2 and could last into December.
James is seeking $250 million in penalties, the estimated benefit derived from the alleged fraud, and a ban on Trump doing business in New York.
James also wants Trump and his three eldest children barred from running a New York company and Trump and the Trump Organization barred from commercial real estate acquisitions for five years.
The lawsuit alleged Trump claimed his Trump Tower penthouse was nearly three times its actual size and valued it at $327 million.
Trump valued Mar-a-Lago at as high as $739 million, more than 10 times a more reasonable estimate, based on residential development that deed terms prohibit, James said.
Manhattan prosecutors had looked into a criminal case over the same conduct but declined to bring one.

James began scrutinizing Trump's business practices in March 2019 after Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth to Deutsche Bank while seeking financing to buy the Buffalo Bills.
Trump has been indicted four times in six months, in Georgia, Washington, D.C., Florida and Manhattan.
The Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud last year and fined $1.6 million; Allen Weisselberg pleaded guilty and served five months in jail.
James' office previously sued over the Trump Foundation; Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to charities and the foundation was shut down.
